newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya drafting bill for anti-corruption authority.
newsitem.headline: Kenya drafting bill for anti-corruption authority.

text.p: Kenya is drafting a bill to set up an anti-graft authority after the International Monetary Fund threatened to drop an aid package unless measures were taken this week.

The independent Daily Nation newspaper on Tuesday quoted Attorney-General Amos Wako as saying he was drafting a bill this week to set up an authority to investigate high-level corruption by individuals with political links.
He said the draft bill would be incorporated in another bill calling for the amendment or repeal of laws the opposition demand be scrapped as repressive before a general election.
Wako said he preferred a comprehensive law against economic crimes but it would take too long.
"I'm moving fast to draft a bill for the cabinet to consider," he said.
No comment was available from other government officials.
The IMF, warning Kenya to make its much-criticised public sector more accountable, said last Thursday a big loan package would lapse unless the government acted by the end of the month.
An IMF spokesman said an IMF mission visited Kenya earlier this month but government measures fell short of expectations.
The IMF extended a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) loan worth $205 million in April last year but regular payments were conditional on Kenya meeting promises on reform.

The last scheduled ESAF payment, a $36 million tranche, was delayed by the IMF for a month from June 30, partly because of concern at the way Kenyan authorities handled the multi-million dollar Goldenberg International financial scandal.
The IMF hit out at the government failure to "take decisive steps to ensure transparency and accountability in the use of public funds and resolve outstanding energy sector reform".
The Daily Nation on Tuesday also quoted Crispus Muititu, the permanent secretary in the Energy Ministry, as saying a bill was being drafted to set up an independent energy regulatory board.
IMF officials said earlier this month the IMF wanted the government to clarify what it planned to do to counter "irregularities" that made the Goldenberg scandal possible.

Goldenberg International was paid about $100 million by the government in 1992 under an export compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya however produces little gold and has no diamond deposits.
The IMF delayed releasing the $36 million ESAF tranche after the high court decided on June 20 to end the prosecution of a businessman and former officials implicated in the scandal.
The opposition cited Goldenberg's alleged links to powerful politicians as the main reason the prosecution was dropped.
